title: Engineering Mechanics: Statics and Dynamics
topics: Kinematics of particles and rigid bodies

notes.body:
Statics deals with bodies that are not accelerating. A force is a bound vector with magnitude, direction and point of application. Work with Cartesian components: F = Fx i + Fy j + Fz k, and resolve every inclined force before summing.

The moment of a force about a point O is M = r × F, where r runs from O to any point on the line of action. In 2D this reduces to M = x·Fy − y·Fx (anticlockwise positive), or simply force × perpendicular distance. A couple is a pair of equal, opposite, non-collinear forces; its moment is the same about every point, so it is a free vector.

Conditions for equilibrium of a rigid body:
- ΣF = 0 and ΣM_O = 0 about any point O
- In 2D that gives three independent scalar equations (ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0, ΣM = 0), so at most three unknown reactions can be found from statics alone
- A particle needs only ΣF = 0 (two equations in 2D)

The free-body diagram (FBD) is the whole method. Isolate the body, replace every support with the reactions it can supply, and include self-weight at the centre of mass:
- Roller or smooth surface: one force normal to the surface
- Pin: two force components
- Fixed (built-in) support: two components plus a moment
- Cable: tension along the cable, pulling away from the body

Useful shortcuts. A two-force member (loaded only at two pins, with no load in between) carries a force along the line joining those pins. A three-force body in equilibrium has forces that are either concurrent or parallel. Lami's theorem: for three concurrent forces, each force divided by the sine of the angle between the other two is the same.

Worked example. A 4 m simply supported beam carries 10 kN at 1.5 m from support A. Moments about A: R_B × 4 = 10 × 1.5, so R_B = 3.75 kN. Vertical equilibrium: R_A = 10 − 3.75 = 6.25 kN. Check with moments about B: 6.25 × 4 = 10 × 2.5 = 25 kN m.

Common pitfalls:
- Leaving forces off the FBD, especially self-weight and the reaction at a pin
- Taking moments about a point that is not on the body, then forgetting to include the moments of all the forces
- Mixing sign conventions between equations. Pick anticlockwise positive and stick to it
- Treating a distributed load as acting at the end, when its resultant acts at the centroid of the load diagram
- A negative answer is not an error. It means the reaction acts the other way from the one you assumed

An ideal truss is made of straight, slender members joined by frictionless pins, with loads applied only at the joints. Each member is therefore a two-force member in pure tension or compression. Real trusses have welded or bolted gusset joints, but the pin-jointed model gives the primary axial forces well.

Determinacy of a plane truss with m members, r reaction components and j joints:
- m + r = 2j: statically determinate (if the geometry is stable)
- m + r > 2j: statically indeterminate (redundant members)
- m + r < 2j: a mechanism
The count is necessary but not sufficient. A truss can satisfy the count and still be unstable if members are badly arranged, for example three collinear members or all reactions concurrent.

Method of joints. Apply ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 at each pin, starting at a joint with no more than two unknowns. Assume every unknown member force is tensile (pulling away from the joint). A negative result means compression.

Method of sections. Cut through no more than three members whose forces you want, and apply three equilibrium equations to one side. Take moments about the point where two of the cut members meet, so that each equation contains a single unknown. This is the quickest way to find one member force deep inside a large truss.

Zero-force members can be spotted by inspection:
- At an unloaded joint with two non-collinear members, both are zero
- At an unloaded joint with three members, two of them collinear, the third is zero
They are not useless. They brace compression members against buckling and carry load when the loading changes.

Frames and machines contain at least one multi-force member (loaded at three or more points, or along its length), so they carry bending. Dismember the structure, draw an FBD of each part, and apply Newton's third law at every connecting pin: equal and opposite forces on the two parts.

Worked example. A bracket has a horizontal member AB, 3 m long, pinned to a wall at A. A strut BC runs from B to a wall pin C, 2 m below A. A 6 kN load hangs at B. At joint B the strut is at θ = tan⁻¹(2/3) to the horizontal. Vertically: F_BC sin θ = 6, so F_BC = 6√13/2 = 10.8 kN (compression). Horizontally: F_AB = F_BC cos θ = 9 kN (tension).

Common pitfalls: getting the arrow direction wrong on the joint FBD, cutting more than three unknown members, and treating a frame member with a mid-span load as a two-force member.

Dry (Coulomb) friction acts tangentially at a contact and opposes the relative sliding, or the tendency to slide.

- Static: F ≤ μs N. The equality holds only when slip is about to happen
- Kinetic: F = μk N once sliding has started, with μk usually a little less than μs
- To a first approximation μ does not depend on the apparent contact area or the sliding speed

The key exam skill is knowing whether F is known. If the body is not at impending motion, F is just another unknown that you find from equilibrium. You then check that F ≤ μs N. Set F = μs N only when the question says slip is impending, or when you are testing an assumed mode of failure.

Angle of friction: φ = tan⁻¹ μs. A block on an incline is on the point of sliding when the incline angle equals φ, which is also called the angle of repose. The total reaction (N and F combined) then makes the angle φ with the normal.

Tipping versus sliding. For a tall block pushed sideways, find the force needed to slide it and the force needed to tip it (normal reaction moved to the edge). The smaller of the two governs.

Wedges and screws. Draw an FBD for each body and put the friction on each surface in the direction that opposes the relative motion at that surface. A square-thread screw behaves like a block on an incline at the helix angle α, where tan α = lead/(π d_mean). The torque to raise a load W is M = W r tan(α + φ). The screw is self-locking if φ > α.

Belt (capstan) friction. For a flat belt or rope on a drum with wrap angle β (in radians), at the point of slip:
- T₂/T₁ = e^(μβ), where T₂ is the tight side
- For a V-belt with groove angle 2γ, replace μ by μ/sin γ
Example: with μ = 0.3 and a half wrap (β = π), T₂/T₁ = e^(0.3π) = 2.57. Two full turns (β = 4π) with μ = 0.25 give e^π = 23.1, which is why a few turns of rope round a bollard hold a ship.

Common pitfalls:
- Automatically writing F = μN
- Drawing friction in the wrong direction. Ask which way the body would move without friction
- Using degrees instead of radians in e^(μβ)
- Forgetting that a rough wall adds a second friction force and makes the problem harder

notes.h: Kinematics of particles and rigid bodies
notes.body:
Kinematics describes motion without asking what causes it.

Rectilinear motion: v = ds/dt and a = dv/dt = v dv/ds. For constant acceleration (and only then): v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as. When a depends on v or s, separate the variables and integrate.

Choose the coordinate system that fits the path:
- Cartesian: the components are independent. In projectile motion with no drag, ax = 0 and ay = −g. Range on level ground R = u² sin 2θ / g. Maximum height H = u² sin²θ / (2g)
- Normal–tangential: a_t = dv/dt along the path, a_n = v²/ρ towards the centre of curvature
- Polar: a_r = r̈ − rθ̇² and a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇. The 2ṙθ̇ term is the Coriolis component

Relative motion: v_B = v_A + v_B/A and a_B = a_A + a_B/A, as vectors.

Rigid bodies in plane motion. Every point shares the same angular velocity ω and angular acceleration α.
- Velocity: v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A, with magnitude ω·AB perpendicular to AB
- Acceleration: a_B = a_A + α × r_B/A − ω² r_B/A. The tangential part is α·AB and the centripetal part is ω²·AB, directed from B to A
- Instantaneous centre of zero velocity (IC): draw perpendiculars to two known velocity directions; they meet at the IC. Then each speed is ω × (distance from the IC). The IC generally has non-zero acceleration, so never use it for accelerations
- Rolling without slip: v_G = ωr and a_G = αr. The contact point is the IC

Rotating reference frames. When a point moves relative to a rotating body:
a = a_O + Ω̇ × r + Ω × (Ω × r) + 2Ω × v_rel + a_rel
Students most often miss the Coriolis term 2Ω × v_rel, for example with a slider moving along a rotating arm.

Worked example. In a slider-crank, crank OA = 0.1 m turns at 120 rev/min (ω = 12.57 rad/s), so v_A = 1.26 m/s perpendicular to OA. Write v_B = v_A + ω_AB × r_B/A, impose the condition that the slider moves only horizontally, and solve for ω_AB and v_B.

Common pitfalls:
- Using the constant-acceleration equations when a varies
- Leaving rev/min unconverted. Multiply by 2π/60 to get rad/s
- Getting the direction of ω²r wrong. It always points towards the reference point
- Applying the IC to accelerations
- Dropping the Coriolis term

Newton's second law for a particle: ΣF = m a, in an inertial frame. For a system of particles or a rigid body, ΣF = m a_G, where G is the centre of mass. Internal forces cancel in pairs (third law).

Method:
- Draw an FBD showing all external forces
- Draw a kinetic diagram showing m a_G, and I_G α for a rigid body
- Choose axes that match the motion (n–t axes for curved paths)
- Write the equations, then add the kinematic constraints (ropes, rolling, linkages)

Rigid body in plane motion:
- ΣFx = m a_Gx and ΣFy = m a_Gy
- ΣM_G = I_G α
- About a fixed pivot O: ΣM_O = I_O α, with I_O = I_G + m d² (parallel-axis theorem)
- About any other point P: ΣM_P = I_G α + (r_G/P × m a_G). This is the moment of the kinetic diagram

Standard I_G values: slender rod mL²/12 (mL²/3 about an end); solid cylinder or disc ½mr²; thin ring mr²; solid sphere (2/5)mr². Radius of gyration k: I = mk².

Connected bodies. Draw a separate FBD for each mass. An ideal string (light, inextensible, over a smooth light pulley) has the same tension throughout and gives equal-magnitude accelerations. For an Atwood machine with masses 5 kg and 3 kg: a = (5 − 3)g/8 = 2.45 m/s², and T = 2(5)(3)g/8 = 36.8 N.

Rolling. If there is no slip, a_G = αr and friction is static, with an unknown value F ≤ μs N. Solve assuming no slip, then check the friction needed. If the check fails, the body slips: put F = μk N and treat a_G and α as independent. A solid cylinder rolling down an incline of angle θ has a = (2/3) g sin θ and needs μs ≥ (1/3) tan θ.

Worked example. A drum (I = 0.6 kg m², r = 0.2 m) is unwound by a hanging 12 kg mass. Mass: mg − T = ma. Drum: Tr = Iα = I a/r. Eliminating T gives a = mg/(m + I/r²) = 117.7/27 = 4.36 m/s², and T = 65.4 N, which is less than the 117.7 N weight, as it should be.

Common pitfalls:
- Putting "ma" on the FBD as if it were a force
- Assuming tension equals weight in accelerating systems
- Taking moments about an accelerating point other than G without the extra m a_G term
- Assuming friction on a rolling body always equals μN
- Getting the sign of the friction force on a rolling body wrong. Assume a direction and let the algebra decide

The work done by a force is U = ∫F · dr. Only the component of force along the displacement does work.
- Weight: U = −mg Δh (independent of the path)
- Linear spring: U = −½k(x₂² − x₁²), where x is the extension measured from the natural length
- Kinetic friction: U = −μk N × (distance slid). It is path-dependent and non-conservative
- Couple: U = ∫M dθ
- Forces that do no work: normal reactions on a fixed smooth surface, static friction at a rolling contact, and the tension in an inextensible string connecting bodies (which does zero net work on the pair)

Work–energy principle: T₁ + ΣU₁→₂ = T₂. Rigid-body kinetic energy: T = ½m v_G² + ½I_G ω², or T = ½I_O ω² for rotation about a fixed axis O.

For conservative forces, define potential energy: V_g = mgh and V_e = ½kx². Then
T₁ + V₁ + U_nc = T₂ + V₂,
where U_nc is the work done by non-conservative forces such as friction, drag and applied motors.

Power is P = F · v = Mω. Mechanical efficiency is η = output power / input power. A car of 1200 kg climbing a 4° slope at 25 m/s against 500 N of resistance needs P = (1200 × 9.81 × sin 4° + 500) × 25 ≈ 33.0 kW at the wheels.

Energy methods give speeds and positions without finding accelerations, and they handle systems of connected bodies neatly. They give no information about forces that do no work, such as a pin reaction. Combine energy with Newton's second law when you need those forces: use energy to find ω, then ΣF = m a_G with the centripetal term.

Worked example. A 0.5 kg ball is fired horizontally by a spring (k = 800 N/m) compressed by 0.15 m. Energy: ½(800)(0.15)² = ½(0.5)v², which gives 9 J = 0.25v², so v = 6.0 m/s.

Second example. A uniform rod of length L, pinned at one end, is released from horizontal. At the vertical position: mg(L/2) = ½(mL²/3)ω², so ω = √(3g/L). The pin force then follows from the centripetal acceleration ω²L/2 = 1.5g. That gives a pin reaction of 2.5mg, not mg.

Common pitfalls:
- Measuring spring extension from the wrong datum
- Forgetting the rotational kinetic energy of wheels and pulleys
- Counting the gravitational potential energy as well as the work done by gravity (double counting)
- Treating the work done by friction on a rolling-without-slip body as non-zero
- Using energy conservation across an impact, where mechanical energy is lost

Integrating Newton's second law over time gives the principle of linear impulse and momentum:
m v₁ + Σ∫F dt = m v₂.
Impulse is a vector, measured in N s. It is the area under the force–time graph. The average force over a contact time Δt is F_avg = Δ(mv)/Δt.

Conservation of linear momentum. If the net external impulse on a system is zero in some direction, the total momentum in that direction is conserved. During short impacts, finite forces such as weight and friction contribute negligible impulse, but impulsive reactions at pins and supports do not. Only directions free of impulsive external forces conserve momentum.

Angular impulse and momentum:
- For a particle, angular momentum about O is H_O = r × mv
- For a rigid body in plane motion, H_G = I_G ω and H_O = I_G ω + (r_G × m v_G). For a fixed axis, H_O = I_O ω
- H₁ + Σ∫M dt = H₂
Angular momentum about a point is conserved when the net external angular impulse about that point is zero. For example, take moments about a fixed pivot: the large pin reaction then has no moment.

Impact. For direct central impact, combine:
- conservation of momentum: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂
- Newton's experimental law: v₂ − v₁ = e(u₁ − u₂), with the coefficient of restitution 0 ≤ e ≤ 1
e = 1 means perfectly elastic (no kinetic energy lost). e = 0 means perfectly plastic (the bodies move off together). For oblique impact, use momentum along the line of impact, use e along the line of impact only, and note that each body's tangential velocity is unchanged if the surfaces are smooth.

Worked example. A 2 kg block at 6 m/s hits a stationary 3 kg block, with e = 0.5.
- Momentum: 12 = 2v₁ + 3v₂
- Restitution: v₂ − v₁ = 3
- Solving gives v₁ = 0.6 m/s and v₂ = 3.6 m/s
- Kinetic energy falls from 36 J to 19.8 J, so 16.2 J is lost

Variable mass. A rocket's thrust is ṁ u_rel. For a jet striking a fixed plate normally, the force is ṁ v.

Common pitfalls:
- Applying energy conservation through an impact
- Sign errors in the restitution equation. Write it as separation speed = e × approach speed
- Conserving linear momentum for a body hit while hinged to a pivot. The pivot supplies an impulse, so conserve angular momentum about the pivot instead
- Forgetting that impulse is a vector, as with a ball that reverses direction

Free undamped vibration of a single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) mass–spring system: m ẍ + kx = 0.
- Natural frequency: ωn = √(k/m) rad/s, fn = ωn/2π Hz, period τ = 2π/ωn
- Solution: x = A sin ωn t + B cos ωn t, with A and B set by the initial displacement and velocity
- For a vertical spring, measure x from the static equilibrium position. Gravity then drops out, and ωn = √(g/δst), where δst is the static deflection

Equivalent springs:
- Parallel: k = k₁ + k₂
- Series: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂
- Cantilever with a tip mass: k = 3EI/L³
- Shaft in torsion: k_t = GJ/L, with ωn = √(k_t/I)
Energy method: T + V = constant. Setting d/dt(T + V) = 0, or Tmax = Vmax (Rayleigh), gives ωn quickly. For a compound pendulum, ωn = √(mgd/I_O).

Viscous damping: m ẍ + c ẋ + kx = 0.
- Critical damping: c_c = 2√(km) = 2mωn. Damping ratio ζ = c/c_c
- Underdamped (ζ < 1): oscillation decays, with damped frequency ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²)
- Critically damped (ζ = 1): fastest return to equilibrium without overshoot
- Overdamped (ζ > 1): slow return, no oscillation
- Logarithmic decrement: δ = ln(x_n/x_(n+1)) = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) ≈ 2πζ for light damping

Harmonic forcing F₀ sin ωt. With frequency ratio r = ω/ωn, the steady-state amplitude is
X = (F₀/k) / √[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²].
- The response peaks near r = 1 (resonance), where X ≈ (F₀/k)/(2ζ)
- The phase lag is 90° at r = 1
- Rotating unbalance m_u e gives F₀ = m_u e ω²

Vibration isolation. The force transmissibility is
TR = √[1 + (2ζr)²] / √[(1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²].
TR < 1 only when r > √2, so isolators need soft mounts (low ωn). Above r = √2, extra damping slightly worsens isolation, but some damping is needed to pass safely through resonance at start-up.

Worked example. With m = 2 kg and k = 800 N/m: ωn = 20 rad/s, fn = 3.18 Hz and c_c = 80 N s/m. If ζ = 0.2, then ωd = 19.6 rad/s and δ = 1.28, so each cycle's amplitude is about 28% of the previous one (e^(−1.28) = 0.28).

Common pitfalls:
- Confusing rad/s with Hz
- Including gravity in the equation of motion when x is measured from static equilibrium
- Combining series springs by simple addition
- Assuming more damping always helps isolation
- Applying the r > √2 rule to amplitude rather than to transmissibility

cards.f: State the equilibrium conditions for a rigid body in 2D.
cards.b: ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0 about any point. That gives three independent equations, so at most three unknowns can be found by statics alone.

cards.f: What is a couple, and why is it called a free vector?
cards.b: A pair of equal, opposite, non-collinear forces. Its moment (force × separation) is the same about every point, so it can be moved anywhere in its plane without changing its effect.

cards.f: How is the moment of a force about a point O defined in vector form?
cards.b: M_O = r × F, where r runs from O to any point on the line of action of F. In 2D, M = x·Fy − y·Fx.

cards.f: What reactions does a fixed (built-in) support supply in 2D?
cards.b: Two force components (horizontal and vertical) and a moment. That is three reaction unknowns in total.

cards.f: What is a two-force member and what does it imply?
cards.b: A body loaded only at two points, with no other loads or moments. For equilibrium the two forces must be equal, opposite and collinear, acting along the line joining the two points.

cards.f: State Lami's theorem.
cards.b: For three concurrent coplanar forces in equilibrium, each force divided by the sine of the angle between the other two forces is the same for all three.

cards.f: A three-force body is in equilibrium. What must be true of the lines of action?
cards.b: They must either meet at a single point (be concurrent) or all be parallel. Otherwise there would be a net moment about the intersection of two of them.

cards.f: Where does the resultant of a triangular distributed load act?
cards.b: At the centroid of the triangle, one third of the span from the larger end. Its magnitude is the area of the load diagram, ½ × w_max × L.

cards.f: You solve for a reaction and get a negative value. What does it mean?
cards.b: The reaction acts opposite to the direction you assumed on the free-body diagram. Its magnitude is still correct, so keep the sign consistent in later equations.

cards.f: What assumptions define an ideal truss?
cards.b: Straight members joined by frictionless pins, with loads applied only at the joints and member self-weight neglected or lumped at the joints. Each member is then a two-force member in pure tension or compression.

cards.f: State the determinacy condition for a plane truss.
cards.b: m + r = 2j for a statically determinate truss (m members, r reactions, j joints). If m + r > 2j the truss is indeterminate; if m + r < 2j it is a mechanism. Stability must still be checked by inspection.

cards.f: When is the method of sections preferred over the method of joints?
cards.b: When you need the force in a few specific members deep inside the truss. One cut through up to three members and a well-chosen moment centre gives each force directly.

cards.f: Name the two rules for identifying zero-force members.
cards.b: (1) At an unloaded joint with two non-collinear members, both carry zero force. (2) At an unloaded joint with three members, two of them collinear, the third carries zero force.

cards.f: Why are zero-force members included in real trusses?
cards.b: They brace compression members against buckling by reducing the effective length. They also carry load under other load cases, and they help the truss keep its shape during erection.

cards.f: Sign convention for member forces in the method of joints?
cards.b: Assume every member is in tension, so its force pulls away from the joint. A positive answer is tension and a negative answer is compression.

cards.f: How does a frame differ from a truss?
cards.b: A frame contains at least one multi-force member, loaded at three or more points or along its length, so that member carries bending as well as axial force. You solve it by dismembering it and applying Newton's third law at the pins.

cards.f: In the method of sections, how should you choose the moment centre?
cards.b: Take moments about the intersection of two of the three cut members. Their forces then drop out and the third force is found in one equation.

cards.f: Can a truss satisfy m + r = 2j and still be unstable?
cards.b: Yes. If the members or reactions are badly arranged, for example all the reactions are parallel or concurrent, or a panel has no diagonal, the truss is a mechanism despite the count.

cards.f: State Coulomb's laws of dry friction.
cards.b: Static friction can take any value up to μs N. When sliding starts, kinetic friction is F = μk N, with μk usually less than μs. To a first approximation μ does not depend on the apparent contact area or the sliding speed.

cards.f: When may you set F = μs N?
cards.b: Only when slip is impending, either because the question says the body is on the point of moving or because you are testing an assumed slip mode. Otherwise F is unknown and must satisfy F ≤ μs N.

cards.f: What is the angle of friction?
cards.b: φ = tan⁻¹ μs. It is the angle between the total contact reaction and the normal at impending slip. A block on an incline starts to slide when the incline angle reaches φ.

cards.f: Give the belt friction equation and say what each symbol means.
cards.b: T₂/T₁ = e^(μβ), where T₂ is the tight-side tension, T₁ the slack-side tension, μ the friction coefficient and β the wrap angle in radians.

cards.f: How does a V-belt modify the belt friction equation?
cards.b: Replace μ by μ/sin γ, where 2γ is the included groove angle. The wedging action raises the normal force, so a V-belt transmits more torque for the same tensions.

cards.f: When is a square-thread screw self-locking?
cards.b: When the friction angle φ is greater than the helix angle α (tan α = lead/(π d_mean)). The load then cannot drive the screw back down by itself.

cards.f: A tall crate is pushed horizontally. How do you decide whether it slides or tips?
cards.b: Find the push needed to slide it (F = μs N) and the push needed to tip it (normal reaction moved to the front edge, moments about that edge). It does whichever needs the smaller push.

cards.f: A rope makes 2 full turns round a post with μ = 0.25. What is T₂/T₁ at slip?
How do you choose the direction of friction on a wedge?
cards.b: On each contact surface, friction opposes the motion of that body relative to the body it touches. Draw a separate FBD for each wedge or block and check each surface on its own.

cards.f: State the three constant-acceleration equations, and when they are valid.
cards.b: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at² and v² = u² + 2as. They are valid only when the acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction.

cards.f: Give the normal and tangential components of acceleration.
cards.b: a_t = dv/dt, along the path. a_n = v²/ρ, towards the centre of curvature, where ρ is the radius of curvature.

cards.f: Give the radial and transverse acceleration in polar coordinates.
cards.b: a_r = r̈ − rθ̇² and a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇. The 2ṙθ̇ term is the Coriolis component.

cards.f: Write the rigid-body velocity relation between two points A and B.
cards.b: v_B = v_A + ω × r_B/A. The relative velocity has magnitude ω·AB and is perpendicular to AB.

cards.f: What is the instantaneous centre of zero velocity, and what is its main limitation?
cards.b: The point (on or off the body) that has zero velocity at that instant, so every point moves as if rotating about it with speed ω × distance. It usually has non-zero acceleration, so it cannot be used for accelerations.

cards.f: Give the rolling-without-slip conditions for a wheel of radius r.
cards.b: v_G = ωr and a_G = αr. The contact point has zero velocity and is the instantaneous centre.

cards.f: Write the acceleration of a point moving relative to a rotating frame.
cards.b: a = a_O + Ω̇ × r + Ω × (Ω × r) + 2Ω × v_rel + a_rel. The 2Ω × v_rel term is the Coriolis acceleration.

cards.f: Give the range of a projectile on level ground, ignoring drag.
cards.b: R = u² sin 2θ / g. The maximum is at θ = 45°. For u = 20 m/s and θ = 30°, R = 400 × sin 60° / 9.81 ≈ 35.3 m.

cards.f: Convert 120 rev/min to rad/s.
State Newton's second law for a rigid body in plane motion.
cards.b: ΣF = m a_G and ΣM_G = I_G α, both in an inertial frame. Moments may also be taken about a fixed pivot O using I_O.

cards.f: State the parallel-axis theorem.
cards.b: I_O = I_G + m d², where d is the distance between the parallel axes through O and G. It applies only when one of the two axes passes through G.

cards.f: Give I_G for a slender rod, a solid disc and a thin ring.
cards.b: Rod: mL²/12 (mL²/3 about an end). Solid disc or cylinder: ½mr². Thin ring: mr².

cards.f: What is the radius of gyration?
cards.b: The distance k at which the whole mass could be concentrated to give the same moment of inertia: I = mk², so k = √(I/m).

cards.f: Find the acceleration of an Atwood machine with masses 5 kg and 3 kg.
cards.b: a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂) = 2g/8 = 2.45 m/s². The tension is 2m₁m₂g/(m₁ + m₂) = 36.8 N.

cards.f: What is the acceleration of a solid cylinder rolling without slip down an incline of angle θ?
cards.b: a = (2/3) g sin θ. Friction is F = (1/3) mg sin θ, so rolling needs μs ≥ (1/3) tan θ.

cards.f: How do you check whether a rolling body slips?
cards.b: Solve assuming no slip (a = αr) to find the friction F needed. If F > μs N, the body slips: set F = μk N and treat a_G and α as independent.

cards.f: Write the moment equation about a general point P that may be accelerating.
cards.b: ΣM_P = I_G α + r_G/P × m a_G. The right-hand side is the moment of the kinetic diagram about P.

cards.f: Why is the tension in a rope supporting an accelerating mass not equal to its weight?
cards.b: From ΣF = ma, T − mg = ma, so T = m(g + a). Tension exceeds the weight when the mass accelerates upwards and is less than the weight when it accelerates downwards.

cards.f: State the work–energy principle with conservative and non-conservative forces separated.
cards.b: T₁ + V₁ + U_nc(1→2) = T₂ + V₂. Here V includes gravitational (mgh) and elastic (½kx²) potential energy, and U_nc is the work of friction, drag and applied forces.

cards.f: Write the kinetic energy of a rigid body in plane motion.
cards.b: T = ½m v_G² + ½I_G ω². For rotation about a fixed axis O this equals ½I_O ω².

cards.f: How much work does a linear spring do as its extension changes from x₁ to x₂?
cards.b: U = −½k(x₂² − x₁²), with x measured from the natural length. The spring does negative work when it is stretched further.

cards.f: Which forces do no work?
cards.b: Normal reactions from fixed smooth surfaces, forces at fixed pins, static friction at a rolling-without-slip contact, and forces always perpendicular to the velocity.

cards.f: Define power and mechanical efficiency.
cards.b: Power is P = F · v (or Mω for rotation), measured in watts. Efficiency η is useful output power divided by input power.

cards.f: Why does friction do no work on a wheel rolling without slip?
cards.b: The contact point has zero velocity at every instant, so the power F · v at the contact is zero.

cards.f: A rod of length L, pinned at one end, falls from horizontal. What is ω at the vertical?
cards.b: mg(L/2) = ½(mL²/3)ω², so ω = √(3g/L).

cards.f: Why can't energy methods give the pin reaction directly?
cards.b: Pin reactions do no work and so do not appear in the energy equation. Find ω or v by energy, then apply ΣF = m a_G, including the centripetal term.

cards.f: Gravitational potential energy or work done by weight: can you use both?
cards.b: Use one or the other. Writing −mgΔh as work and also including mgh as potential energy counts gravity twice.

cards.f: State the principle of linear impulse and momentum.
cards.b: m v₁ + Σ∫F dt = m v₂. Impulse is a vector, measured in N s, equal to the area under the force–time graph.

cards.f: When is linear momentum conserved?
cards.b: In any direction in which the net external impulse on the system is zero. During short impacts this means directions with no impulsive external reactions.

cards.f: Define the coefficient of restitution.
cards.b: e = (separation speed along the line of impact)/(approach speed along the line of impact). e = 1 is perfectly elastic and e = 0 is perfectly plastic.

cards.f: In smooth oblique impact, which velocity components change?
cards.b: Only the components along the line of impact (the common normal). Each body's tangential component stays the same because a smooth contact gives no tangential impulse.

cards.f: When should angular momentum be conserved instead of linear momentum?
cards.b: When the body is pivoted, because the pivot supplies an unknown impulsive reaction. Take angular momentum about the pivot, where that reaction has no moment.

cards.f: Write the angular momentum of a rigid body about a fixed axis O.
cards.b: H_O = I_O ω. For general plane motion, H_O = I_G ω + (r_G × m v_G).

cards.f: A 0.4 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds at 6 m/s. What impulse does the wall give?
cards.b: Taking the rebound direction as positive, Δ(mv) = 0.4 × 6 − 0.4 × (−10) = 6.4 N s, directed away from the wall.

cards.f: Is mechanical energy conserved in an impact?
cards.b: Only if e = 1. Otherwise kinetic energy is lost to deformation, heat and sound, so energy conservation cannot be applied across the impact itself.

cards.f: What is the force on a fixed plate struck normally by a water jet that spreads out sideways?
cards.b: F = ṁ v, where ṁ is the mass flow rate and v the jet speed, because the normal momentum of the jet is reduced to zero.

cards.f: Give the natural frequency of a mass–spring system in rad/s and Hz.
cards.b: ωn = √(k/m) rad/s and fn = ωn/2π Hz. The period is τ = 1/fn.

cards.f: How can ωn be found from the static deflection?
cards.b: ωn = √(g/δst), because kδst = mg. This holds for any linear spring loaded by gravity.

cards.f: How do springs combine in series and in parallel?
cards.b: Parallel: k = k₁ + k₂. Series: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂, so two equal springs in series give half the stiffness.

cards.f: Define critical damping and damping ratio.
cards.b: Critical damping c_c = 2√(km) = 2mωn is the smallest damping that prevents oscillation. The damping ratio is ζ = c/c_c.

cards.f: Give the damped natural frequency.
cards.b: ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²), valid for underdamped systems (ζ < 1).

cards.f: Define the logarithmic decrement and link it to ζ.
cards.b: δ = ln(x_n/x_(n+1)) for successive peaks. δ = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²), which is about 2πζ for light damping.

cards.f: At what frequency ratio does transmissibility drop below 1?
cards.b: r = ω/ωn > √2, whatever the damping. Effective isolators therefore use soft mounts so that ωn is well below the forcing frequency.

cards.f: What is the phase lag of the response at resonance (r = 1)?
cards.b: 90° for any damping ratio. The response lags the force by a quarter cycle.

cards.f: Why can extra damping be undesirable above r = √2?
cards.b: In that region, transmissibility rises as ζ increases, so more damping lets more force through. Damping is still needed to limit the response when passing through resonance.

questions.q: How many independent scalar equilibrium equations are available for a single rigid body loaded in a plane?
questions.why: In 2D, ΣFx = 0, ΣFy = 0 and ΣM = 0 give three independent equations. Six is the number for a body in 3D.

questions.q: At an unloaded truss joint, three members meet. Two are collinear and the third is inclined at 50° to them. What is the force in the inclined member?
options: Equal to the force in each collinear member
Half the force in the collinear members
It cannot be found without the external loads
questions.why: Resolving perpendicular to the collinear pair, only the inclined member has a component in that direction, so its force must be zero.

questions.q: A 10 kg block rests without moving on a 30° incline. The coefficient of static friction is 0.6. What is the friction force on the block? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
questions.why: The block is in equilibrium, so F balances the component of weight down the slope: mg sin 30° = 49.1 N. The 51.0 N figure is μs N, the limiting value, which is not reached.

questions.q: A car travels round a bend of radius 50 m at a constant 20 m/s. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?
questions.why: The speed is constant, so a_t = 0, but a_n = v²/ρ = 400/50 = 8 m/s² towards the centre of the bend.

questions.q: The instantaneous centre of zero velocity of a link in plane motion can be used to find which of the following directly?
options: Velocities of points on the link
Accelerations of points on the link
Neither, as it only locates the centre of mass
questions.why: Every point's velocity is ω × (distance from the IC), but the IC itself generally accelerates, so it cannot be used for accelerations.

questions.q: A thin ring and a solid disc of the same mass and radius are released together from rest and roll without slipping down the same incline. Which statement is correct?
options: The ring reaches the bottom first
The disc reaches the bottom first
They arrive together because the mass and radius are equal
questions.why: a = g sin θ/(1 + k²/r²). The disc has k²/r² = ½ and the ring has k²/r² = 1, so the disc accelerates faster (2/3 g sin θ against ½ g sin θ).

questions.q: A uniform solid sphere rolls without slipping down an incline of angle θ. What minimum coefficient of static friction is needed?
questions.why: With I = (2/5)mr², a = (5/7) g sin θ and F = mg sin θ − ma = (2/7) mg sin θ. Dividing by N = mg cos θ gives μ ≥ (2/7) tan θ. One third of tan θ is the result for a solid cylinder.

questions.q: A wheel rolls without slipping down a rough slope. Which force does work on the wheel?
options: The static friction force at the contact
questions.why: The weight does work as the centre drops. The normal reaction is perpendicular to the motion, and friction acts at a point with zero velocity, so neither does work.

questions.q: Two bodies collide directly with a coefficient of restitution e = 0. Which statement is true?
options: The bodies move off with a common velocity
The bodies reverse direction with equal speeds
questions.why: e = 0 means zero separation speed, so the bodies move together (perfectly plastic). Momentum is still conserved, but kinetic energy is lost.

questions.q: A uniform rod hangs from a fixed frictionless pivot and is struck horizontally by a small particle that sticks to it. Which quantity is conserved during the impact?
options: Linear momentum of the rod and particle
Kinetic energy of the rod and particle
Angular momentum of the rod and particle about the pivot
Angular momentum about the centre of mass of the rod
questions.why: The pivot supplies an impulsive reaction, so linear momentum is not conserved. That reaction has no moment about the pivot, so angular momentum about the pivot is conserved.

questions.q: The mass on a spring is doubled while the stiffness stays the same. What happens to the undamped natural frequency?
options: It falls by a factor of √2
questions.why: ωn = √(k/m), so doubling m multiplies ωn by 1/√2.

questions.q: For a damped spring-mounted machine under harmonic excitation, when is the force transmitted to the foundation less than the applied force?
questions.why: TR < 1 only for r > √2, whatever the damping ratio. This is why isolators are designed with a low natural frequency.

questions.q: A force F = (−120 i + 160 j) N acts at the point (3, 2) m relative to origin O. Find the moment of F about O and the perpendicular distance from O to its line of action.
markScheme: Uses M = x·Fy − y·Fx (or r × F)
M = 3(160) − 2(−120) = 720 N m, anticlockwise (+k)
questions.modelAnswer: In 2D, M_O = x·Fy − y·Fx = 3 × 160 − 2 × (−120) = 480 + 240 = 720 N m. The answer is positive, so the moment is anticlockwise (along +k). The magnitude of the force is √(120² + 160²) = 200 N. Since M = F·d, the perpendicular distance from O to the line of action is 720/200 = 3.6 m.

questions.q: A plane truss has 11 members and 7 joints. It rests on a pin at one end and a roller at the other. Classify its determinacy, and explain why this count alone does not prove the truss can carry load.
markScheme: r = 3 (pin 2 + roller 1)
So it is statically determinate, provided it is stable
The count is necessary but not sufficient. A badly arranged truss (e.g. a panel with no diagonal while another has a redundant member, or concurrent or parallel reactions) can be a mechanism
questions.modelAnswer: The pin supplies two reactions and the roller one, so r = 3. Then m + r = 11 + 3 = 14, which equals 2j = 14, so the truss meets the condition for static determinacy. The count only compares the number of unknowns with the number of joint equations, though. If members are arranged poorly, for example one panel lacks a diagonal while another has two, or the reactions are parallel or concurrent, the structure can still be a mechanism or partly unstable. Stability has to be checked by inspection.

questions.q: A sailor holds a load of 2000 N with a rope wrapped two full turns around a fixed bollard. The coefficient of friction is 0.25. What is the smallest force the sailor must apply to stop the rope slipping?
markScheme: β = 2 × 2π = 4π rad
T₂/T₁ = e^(μβ) = e^π ≈ 23.1, with T₂ = 2000 N as the tight side
questions.modelAnswer: The wrap angle is two full turns, β = 4π rad. At impending slip, T₂/T₁ = e^(μβ) = e^(0.25 × 4π) = e^π ≈ 23.14. The load side is the tight side, T₂ = 2000 N, so the holding force is T₁ = 2000/23.14 ≈ 86.4 N. Friction multiplies the sailor's pull by more than twenty, which is why a few turns on a bollard can hold a large load.

questions.q: A 20 kg crate is pushed up a 25° incline at constant speed by a force parallel to the slope. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.3. Find the force needed. (g = 9.81 m/s²)
markScheme: N = mg cos 25° = 177.8 N
Friction down the slope = μk N = 53.3 N
questions.modelAnswer: Constant speed means zero acceleration, so the forces along and normal to the slope balance. Normal to the slope: N = 20 × 9.81 × cos 25° = 177.8 N. The crate moves up the slope, so kinetic friction acts down the slope with magnitude 0.3 × 177.8 = 53.3 N. Along the slope: P = mg sin 25° + 53.3 = 82.9 + 53.3 ≈ 136.3 N.

questions.q: A ball is projected from level ground at 20 m/s and 30° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, find the time of flight, the range and the maximum height. (g = 9.81 m/s²)
markScheme: Time of flight = 2u sin θ/g = 2.04 s
R = u² sin 2θ/g = 35.3 m
H = u² sin²θ/(2g) = 5.10 m
questions.modelAnswer: The vertical component is 20 sin 30° = 10 m/s and the horizontal component is 20 cos 30° = 17.32 m/s. The time of flight is 2 × 10/9.81 = 2.04 s. The range is 17.32 × 2.04 = 35.3 m, which agrees with u² sin 2θ/g = 400 sin 60°/9.81. The maximum height is 10²/(2 × 9.81) = 5.10 m.

questions.q: A car on a bend of radius 80 m is travelling at 15 m/s and speeding up at 2 m/s². Find the magnitude of its total acceleration.
markScheme: a_t = 2 m/s² along the path
a_n = v²/ρ = 225/80 = 2.81 m/s² towards the centre
questions.modelAnswer: Use normal–tangential components. The tangential component is the rate of change of speed, a_t = 2 m/s². The normal component is a_n = v²/ρ = 15²/80 = 2.81 m/s², directed towards the centre of the bend. The two are perpendicular, so |a| = √(2² + 2.81²) = 3.45 m/s².

questions.q: A 70 kg passenger stands on a scale in a lift that is accelerating upwards at 1.5 m/s². What does the scale read, in newtons? (g = 9.81 m/s²)
markScheme: N − mg = ma written with up positive
questions.modelAnswer: The passenger's FBD shows the weight mg acting down and the scale force N acting up. Newton's second law with up positive gives N − mg = ma, so N = m(g + a) = 70 × 11.31 ≈ 792 N. That is more than the 687 N weight, so the passenger feels heavier.

questions.q: A 1200 kg car climbs a 4° slope at a steady 25 m/s against a constant resistance of 500 N. Find the power delivered at the wheels. (g = 9.81 m/s²)
markScheme: Weight component = 1200 × 9.81 × sin 4° = 821 N
Driving force = 821 + 500 = 1321 N (steady speed)
questions.modelAnswer: At steady speed the driving force balances the component of weight down the slope plus the resistance. The weight component is 1200 × 9.81 × sin 4° = 821 N, so the driving force is 821 + 500 = 1321 N. Power is P = F·v = 1321 × 25 ≈ 33,000 W, or 33.0 kW.

questions.q: A 0.15 kg cricket ball arrives at 30 m/s and leaves the bat in the opposite direction at 40 m/s. Contact lasts 2 ms. Find the impulse and the average force on the ball.
markScheme: Takes the rebound direction as positive: Δv = 40 − (−30) = 70 m/s
Impulse = mΔv = 10.5 N s
questions.modelAnswer: Take the direction the ball leaves the bat as positive. Its velocity changes from −30 m/s to +40 m/s, so Δv = 70 m/s. The impulse is m Δv = 0.15 × 70 = 10.5 N s, in the direction of the rebound. The average force is impulse divided by contact time: 10.5/0.002 = 5250 N, about 5.3 kN. Weight is negligible over this short time.

questions.q: A 4 kg mass hangs from two springs connected in series, with stiffnesses 3000 N/m and 6000 N/m. Find the equivalent stiffness, the static deflection and the natural frequency in Hz. (g = 9.81 m/s²)
questions.modelAnswer: Springs in series carry the same force, so their compliances add: 1/k = 1/3000 + 1/6000 = 1/2000, giving k = 2000 N/m. The static deflection is mg/k = 4 × 9.81/2000 = 0.0196 m, or 19.6 mm. The natural frequency is ωn = √(k/m) = √500 = 22.4 rad/s, so fn = 22.36/(2π) = 3.56 Hz. As a check, √(g/δst) = √(9.81/0.0196) = 22.4 rad/s.

questions.q: A uniform horizontal beam AB is 3.0 m long and has a mass of 20 kg. End A is pinned to a vertical wall. End B is held by a light cable BC, attached to the wall at C, 2.0 m directly above A. A shop sign of mass 40 kg hangs from the beam 2.5 m from A. Owner Priya Shah wants to check the fixings. (a) Draw and describe the free-body diagram of the beam. (b) Find the tension in the cable. (c) Find the horizontal and vertical components of the pin reaction at A, and its magnitude. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
markScheme: FBD: weight 196.2 N at 1.5 m, sign 392.4 N at 2.5 m, cable tension T along BC, pin components Ax and Ay at A
Cable angle: tan θ = 2/3, θ = 33.7°, sin θ = 0.555
Moments about A eliminate Ax and Ay
T sin θ = 425.1 N, so T = 766 N
ΣFx: Ax = T cos θ = 638 N (wall pushes the beam away from the wall)
ΣFy: Ay = 588.6 − 425.1 = 163.5 N upwards
Check with moments about B or C
Clear sign convention and units throughout
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Isolate the beam. The forces on it are: its weight, 20 × 9.81 = 196.2 N, at the midpoint 1.5 m from A; the sign, 40 × 9.81 = 392.4 N, at 2.5 m; the cable tension T, acting along BC from B towards C; and the pin reaction at A, shown as unknown components Ax (horizontal) and Ay (vertical).

(b) The cable rises 2.0 m over a horizontal run of 3.0 m, so tan θ = 2/3 and θ = 33.7°. Then sin θ = 2/√13 = 0.555 and cos θ = 3/√13 = 0.832. Taking moments about A removes both pin components. Only the vertical part of T has a moment about A, with lever arm 3.0 m:
T sin θ × 3.0 = 196.2 × 1.5 + 392.4 × 2.5 = 294.3 + 981.0 = 1275.3 N m.
So T sin θ = 425.1 N and T = 425.1/0.555 = 766 N.

(c) Horizontal equilibrium: the horizontal part of T pulls B towards the wall, so the pin must push the beam away from the wall. Ax = T cos θ = 766 × 0.832 = 638 N.
Vertical equilibrium: Ay + T sin θ = 196.2 + 392.4, so Ay = 588.6 − 425.1 = 163.5 N, acting upwards.
The magnitude of the pin reaction is √(638² + 163.5²) ≈ 658 N, at tan⁻¹(163.5/638) = 14.4° above the horizontal.

Check. Take moments about C, where T has no moment. The forces with moments about C are Ax (lever arm 2.0 m) and the two weights. Ax × 2.0 = 1275.3 gives Ax = 638 N, which agrees with the result above.

For the fixings, the cable anchor must carry about 0.77 kN and the wall pin about 0.66 kN, mostly in compression of the beam into the wall. Ms Shah should add a suitable safety factor to these values.

questions.q: A bridge truss spans 12 m between a pin at A and a roller at E. The bottom chord joints are A, B, C, D and E, at 3 m spacing. The top chord joints are F, G and H, 3 m directly above B, C and D. The members are AB, BC, CD, DE, FG, GH, AF, EH, BF, CG, DH, FC and HC. Loads of 20 kN act downwards at each of B, C and D. (a) Show that the truss is statically determinate. (b) Using the method of sections, find the forces in FG, FC and BC. (c) Identify a zero-force member and find the forces in AF and BF.
markScheme: Symmetry gives R_A = R_E = 30 kN
Section cut through FG, FC and BC, left part used
Moments about C: 3F_FG + 30 × 6 − 20 × 3 = 0, so F_FG = −40 kN (40 kN compression)
Moments about F: 3F_BC = 30 × 3, so F_BC = 30 kN tension
Vertical: 30 − 20 − F_FC/√2 = 0, so F_FC = 14.1 kN tension
Horizontal check: −40 + 30 + 10 = 0
CG is a zero-force member: joint G is unloaded and FG, GH are collinear
Joint A: F_AF sin 45° = −30 gives AF = 42.4 kN compression, with AB = 30 kN tension
Joint B: BF = 20 kN tension
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) There are 13 members and 8 joints, and the pin plus roller give r = 3. Since m + r = 16 = 2j, the truss is statically determinate. The panels are fully triangulated, so it is also stable.

Reactions. Both the loads and the geometry are symmetrical, so R_A = R_E = 60/2 = 30 kN, and the pin has no horizontal reaction.

(b) Cut through FG, FC and BC, between B and C, and keep the left part (joints A, B and F). Assume every cut member is in tension.
- Moments about C (6, 0), where FC and BC meet: FG acts horizontally at a height of 3 m. Taking anticlockwise as positive, −3F_FG − 30 × 6 + 20 × 3 = 0, so F_FG = −40 kN. FG is in 40 kN compression.
- Moments about F (3, 3), where FG and FC meet: BC acts at a lever arm of 3 m. 3F_BC − 30 × 3 = 0, so F_BC = 30 kN (tension). The 20 kN load at B passes through F's vertical line and has no moment.
- Vertical forces: FC runs at 45° down towards C. 30 − 20 − F_FC sin 45° = 0, so F_FC = 10√2 = 14.1 kN (tension).
- Horizontal check: F_FG + F_BC + F_FC cos 45° = −40 + 30 + 10 = 0. ✓

(c) At joint G, the members FG and GH are collinear and no load acts there. Resolving vertically, the force in CG must be zero.
At joint A, AF is inclined at 45°. Vertically: 30 + F_AF sin 45° = 0, so F_AF = −42.4 kN, which is 42.4 kN compression. Horizontally: F_AB = 30 kN tension.
At joint B, AB and BC are collinear and BF is vertical, so BF carries the 20 kN load: BF = 20 kN in tension.

Equilibrium check at F. The forces on the joint are AF (+30, +30), BF (0, −20), FG (−40, 0) and FC (+10, −10). Both components sum to zero, which confirms the results.

questions.q: A uniform ladder 5.0 m long with a mass of 15 kg rests against a smooth vertical wall at 60° to the horizontal floor. The coefficient of static friction between the ladder and the floor is 0.35. A decorator, Tom Reilly (75 kg), climbs the ladder. (a) Show that the ladder alone will not slip. (b) Find how far up the ladder Tom can climb before it slips. (c) Suggest two practical ways to let him reach the top safely, and justify one with reference to your analysis. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
markScheme: FBD: wall reaction P horizontal; floor N and F; weights at the midpoint and at distance s along the ladder
Ladder alone: moments about the foot give P = 15g × 1.25/(5 sin 60°) = 42.5 N
Friction needed = 42.5 N; μ needed = 0.289 < 0.35, so it is safe
With Tom: N = 90g = 882.9 N
At slip F = μN = 309.0 N, and F = P by horizontal equilibrium
Moments about the foot: P × 5 sin 60° = 15g × 2.5 cos 60° + 75g × s cos 60°
He can climb about 3.1 m of the 5 m ladder
Remedies: steeper angle, a person footing the ladder, anti-slip feet or a higher-μ base, tying the top
Justification linked to the moment arms or the friction limit
questions.modelAnswer:
The forces on the ladder are the wall reaction P, which is horizontal because the wall is smooth; the floor reaction N; floor friction F, acting away from the wall; the ladder's weight 15g = 147.2 N at its midpoint; and Tom's weight 75g = 735.8 N at distance s along the ladder from the foot.

(a) Ladder alone. Take moments about the foot. P acts at a height of 5 sin 60° = 4.33 m, and the ladder's weight acts at a horizontal distance of 2.5 cos 60° = 1.25 m.
P × 4.33 = 147.2 × 1.25, so P = 42.5 N.
Horizontal equilibrium gives F = P = 42.5 N, and N = 147.2 N. The ratio F/N needed is 0.289, which is less than 0.35, so the ladder stands safely.

(b) With Tom on the ladder, N = 90 × 9.81 = 882.9 N wherever he stands. The greatest friction available is 0.35 × 882.9 = 309.0 N. At impending slip F = P = 309.0 N. Moments about the foot:
309.0 × 4.33 = 147.2 × 1.25 + 735.8 × s cos 60°
1338.1 = 183.9 + 367.9 s
s = 3.14 m.
Tom can climb about 3.1 m along the 5 m ladder before it slips. The ladder is unsafe for work near the top.

(c) Possible remedies:
- Set the ladder steeper (about 4 up to 1 out, roughly 75°).
- Have a second person foot it, fit anti-slip feet, or tie the top.
A steeper ladder reduces cos θ, which shortens the horizontal lever arms of both weights about the foot. It also raises the wall contact, increasing sin θ. Both effects reduce the wall reaction P that friction must balance. At 75°, repeating the analysis with Tom at the top (s = 5 m) gives P = (15g × 2.5 + 75g × 5) cos 75°/(5 sin 75°) ≈ 217 N. That is less than the 309 N available, so he could reach the top.

questions.q: In the slider-crank mechanism of a compressor, the crank OA is 100 mm long and rotates anticlockwise at a constant 120 rev/min about the fixed point O. The connecting rod AB is 300 mm long. Piston B moves along a horizontal line through O. When the crank is at 60° above the horizontal, on the same side as B: (a) find the velocity of A; (b) find the angular velocity of AB; (c) find the velocity of the piston B. (d) Explain how you would go on to find the piston's acceleration, naming the terms involved.
markScheme: v_B = v_A + ω_AB × r_B/A, so ω_AB × r = (0.0866ω_AB, 0.287ω_AB)
Vertical component of v_B is zero: 0.628 + 0.287ω_AB = 0
ω_AB = −2.19 rad/s, i.e. 2.19 rad/s clockwise
Acceleration: a_B = a_A + α_AB × r_B/A − ω_AB² r_B/A
a_A is purely centripetal, ω² × OA = 15.8 m/s² towards O, since the crank speed is constant
Unknowns α_AB and a_B are found from the two components
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Convert the crank speed: ω = 120 × 2π/60 = 12.57 rad/s. Place O at the origin. Then A = (0.1 cos 60°, 0.1 sin 60°) = (0.050, 0.0866) m. A moves on a circle, so v_A = ω × OA = 12.57 × 0.1 = 1.257 m/s, perpendicular to OA. For anticlockwise rotation, v_A = ωk × r_A = (−1.088, 0.628) m/s.

(b) Find the geometry first. B lies on the x-axis at x_B = 0.050 + √(0.3² − 0.0866²) = 0.050 + 0.287 = 0.337 m. So r_B/A = (0.287, −0.0866) m, and the rod makes 16.8° with the horizontal.
The rigid-body relation is v_B = v_A + ω_AB k × r_B/A. Here k × (x, y) = (−y, x), so ω_AB k × r_B/A = (0.0866ω_AB, 0.287ω_AB).
B is constrained to move horizontally, so the j-component of v_B is zero:
0.628 + 0.287ω_AB = 0, giving ω_AB = −2.19 rad/s.
The negative sign means the rod turns clockwise at 2.19 rad/s.

(c) The i-component gives v_B = −1.088 + 0.0866 × (−2.19) = −1.28 m/s. The piston is moving towards O at 1.28 m/s.
Check by instantaneous centre. The IC of AB lies where the line OA extended meets the vertical through B. Its distances give v_A/IA = v_B/IB = ω_AB, which reproduces the same values.

(d) For accelerations, use a_B = a_A + α_AB k × r_B/A − ω_AB² r_B/A.
- The crank speed is constant, so a_A is purely centripetal: ω² × OA = 15.8 m/s², directed from A to O.
- The term −ω_AB² r_B/A has magnitude 2.19² × 0.3 = 1.44 m/s², directed from B to A.
- The tangential term α_AB × AB is perpendicular to AB, with α_AB unknown.
Requiring a_B to be horizontal gives α_AB from the j-component, and the i-component then gives the piston acceleration. The instantaneous centre must not be used for this step.

questions.q: Block A (10 kg) sits on a rough plane inclined at 30°. It is attached by a light inextensible rope, running parallel to the plane over a smooth light pulley at the top, to block B (8 kg), which hangs freely. The coefficients of friction between A and the plane are μs = 0.25 and μk = 0.20. The system is released from rest. (a) Show that the system moves, and state the direction. (b) Find the acceleration and the rope tension. (c) Find B's speed after it has fallen 1.5 m. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
markScheme: FBDs of both blocks; same tension and same magnitude of acceleration
Driving force if A moves up: m_B g − m_A g sin 30° = 78.48 − 49.05 = 29.43 N
Maximum static friction = 0.25 × 10g cos 30° = 21.24 N < 29.43 N, so A slides up the slope
Kinetic friction = 0.20 × 84.96 = 16.99 N, acting down the slope on A
T = 8(9.81 − 0.691) = 73.0 N, checked with block A
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) First check whether the system moves. If A slid up the slope, the net driving force before friction would be m_B g − m_A g sin 30° = 78.48 − 49.05 = 29.43 N. The normal force on A is N = 10 × 9.81 × cos 30° = 84.96 N, so the greatest static friction is 0.25 × 84.96 = 21.24 N. That is less than 29.43 N, so the system cannot stay at rest. A slides up the slope and B falls.

(b) Once sliding starts, kinetic friction 0.20 × 84.96 = 16.99 N acts down the slope on A. The rope is light and inextensible and the pulley is smooth, so both blocks have the same tension T and the same magnitude of acceleration a.
- Block B, taking down as positive: 8(9.81) − T = 8a
- Block A, taking up the slope as positive: T − 10(9.81) sin 30° − 16.99 = 10a
Adding the equations eliminates T: 78.48 − 49.05 − 16.99 = 18a, so a = 12.44/18 = 0.691 m/s².
Then T = 8(9.81 − 0.691) = 73.0 N. Check with block A: 10 × 0.691 + 49.05 + 16.99 = 73.0 N. ✓
As expected, the tension lies between A's resistance (66.0 N) and B's weight (78.5 N).

(c) The acceleration is constant, so v² = u² + 2as = 0 + 2 × 0.691 × 1.5 = 2.073, giving v = 1.44 m/s.
Energy check. The loss of potential energy of B is 8g × 1.5 = 117.7 J. The gain of potential energy of A is 10g × 1.5 sin 30° = 73.6 J, and the friction work is 16.99 × 1.5 = 25.5 J. The kinetic energy is therefore 117.7 − 73.6 − 25.5 = 18.6 J. Since ½ × 18 × v² = 18.6 J, v = 1.44 m/s, which agrees.

questions.q: A solid uniform cylinder of mass 20 kg and radius 0.15 m is released from rest on a slope inclined at 25°. The coefficients of friction are μs = 0.12 and μk = 0.10. (a) Assuming rolling without slip, find the acceleration of the centre and the friction force needed. (b) Show that the cylinder cannot roll without slipping. (c) Find the actual linear acceleration of the centre and the angular acceleration. (d) Explain how a_G and αr compare, and what this tells you about the contact point. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
markScheme: FBD: mg, N normal to the slope, F up the slope at the contact
No-slip: mg sin θ − F = ma, Fr = ½mr²α, a = αr
Friction needed / N = 0.155 > μs = 0.12, so the cylinder slips
Slipping: F = μk N = 17.8 N up the slope
a_G = g sin 25° − μk g cos 25° = 3.26 m/s²
αr = 1.78 m/s² < a_G = 3.26 m/s²
So the contact point slides down the slope relative to the surface, which agrees with friction acting up the slope
questions.modelAnswer:
Take axes along and normal to the slope. The forces on the cylinder are its weight mg = 196.2 N, the normal reaction N and friction F at the contact. Assume F acts up the slope, which it must do to produce clockwise spin for a cylinder rolling down. The moment of inertia is I_G = ½mr² = 0.5 × 20 × 0.15² = 0.225 kg m².

(a) The equations are:
- along the slope: mg sin θ − F = ma
- moments about G: Fr = I_G α
- rolling condition: a = αr
Combining them gives F = ½ma, so a = (2/3) g sin 25° = (2/3)(9.81)(0.4226) = 2.76 m/s². The friction needed is F = ½ × 20 × 2.76 = 27.6 N.

(b) Normal to the slope, N = mg cos 25° = 196.2 × 0.9063 = 177.8 N. The greatest static friction available is 0.12 × 177.8 = 21.3 N. Rolling needs 27.6 N, which is more than this. Put another way, rolling needs μs ≥ (1/3) tan 25° = 0.155, but μs is only 0.12. The cylinder therefore slips.

(c) While slipping, friction is kinetic: F = μk N = 0.10 × 177.8 = 17.8 N, acting up the slope. The linear and angular motions are now independent:
a_G = g sin 25° − μk g cos 25° = 4.146 − 0.889 = 3.26 m/s²
α = Fr/I_G = 17.8 × 0.15/0.225 = 11.9 rad/s²

(d) The contact point's velocity is v_G − ωr, which changes at the rate a_G − αr = 3.26 − 1.78 = 1.48 m/s² down the slope. Starting from rest, the contact point therefore slides down the slope relative to the surface. Kinetic friction opposes this sliding, so it acts up the slope, which agrees with the direction assumed. The slip speed keeps growing for as long as the cylinder stays on this slope, so it never settles into pure rolling. The kinetic friction does negative work throughout, so mechanical energy is not conserved.

questions.q: A 4 kg package is released from rest on a ramp inclined at 30°. It slides 2.0 m down the ramp and then meets a buffer spring of stiffness 2000 N/m, aligned with the ramp. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.15 throughout. (a) Find the package's speed just before it hits the spring. (b) Find the maximum compression of the spring. (c) Will the package rebound up the ramp? Justify your answer quantitatively, given μs = 0.20. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
markScheme: Net force along the slope while sliding down = mg sin 30° − μk mg cos 30° = 19.62 − 5.10 = 14.52 N
Work–energy over 2 m: 14.52 × 2 = ½ × 4 × v²
Energy equation to maximum compression x: 14.52(2 + x) = ½(2000)x²
x = 0.178 m (positive root)
At maximum compression the spring force kx = 356 N
Down-slope weight component 19.6 N plus the greatest static friction 6.8 N is much less than 356 N, so the package rebounds
Correct handling of the direction of friction on the rebound (friction now acts down the slope)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) While the package slides down, kinetic friction acts up the slope. The normal force is mg cos 30° = 4 × 9.81 × 0.866 = 33.98 N, so friction is 0.15 × 33.98 = 5.10 N. The component of weight down the slope is 4 × 9.81 × 0.5 = 19.62 N. The net force along the slope is 14.52 N, and it is constant.
Work–energy from rest over 2.0 m: 14.52 × 2.0 = ½ × 4 × v², so v² = 14.52 and v = 3.81 m/s.

(b) Let the maximum compression be x. Between release and maximum compression the package starts and finishes at rest. Gravity and friction do net work 14.52(2.0 + x), and all of it is stored in the spring:
14.52(2.0 + x) = ½ × 2000 × x²
1000x² − 14.52x − 29.04 = 0
x = [14.52 + √(14.52² + 4 × 1000 × 29.04)]/2000 = (14.52 + 341.1)/2000 = 0.178 m.
Check: ½ × 2000 × 0.178² = 31.6 J, and 14.52 × 2.178 = 31.6 J. ✓

(c) At maximum compression the package is momentarily at rest. The spring pushes it up the slope with force kx = 2000 × 0.178 = 356 N. Resisting this is the down-slope weight component, 19.6 N, plus static friction, which can now act down the slope and is at most 0.20 × 33.98 = 6.8 N. The total resistance is at most 26.4 N, far less than 356 N, so the package will rebound.

To estimate how far it rebounds: on the way up, kinetic friction (5.10 N) and the weight component (19.62 N) both act down the slope, a total of 24.72 N. The package leaves the spring with 31.6 − 24.72 × 0.178 = 27.2 J. It then travels about 27.2/24.72 ≈ 1.1 m up the ramp. Since tan 30° = 0.577 > μs = 0.20, it cannot stay there, and it slides back down again. Friction dissipates energy on every pass, so the package eventually settles against the spring.

questions.q: A uniform slender rod of length 1.2 m and mass 3 kg is pinned at one end, O, to a frictionless horizontal axle. It is held horizontal and released from rest. (a) Find the angular acceleration and the pin reaction just after release. (b) Using energy, find the angular velocity when the rod hangs vertically. (c) Find the pin reaction at that instant, and comment on the result. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
markScheme: I_O = mL²/3 = 1.44 kg m²
At release: ΣM_O = mg L/2 = I_O α, so α = 3g/(2L) = 12.3 rad/s²
a_G = αL/2 = 7.36 m/s² downward, with ω = 0 so there is no centripetal term
Pin reaction: mg − R = m a_G, so R = 7.36 N upward (= mg/4)
Energy: mg L/2 = ½ I_O ω²
At the vertical α = 0, since weight has no moment about O
a_G = ω²L/2 = 14.7 m/s² upward, towards O
R − mg = m ω² L/2, so R = 73.6 N (= 2.5mg)
Comment: the pin force varies widely; design for 2.5mg, not for the static weight
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) About the fixed pivot, I_O = mL²/3 = 3 × 1.2²/3 = 1.44 kg m². Just after release ω = 0, so G has no centripetal acceleration. The only moment about O is from the weight: ΣM_O = mg(L/2) = 3 × 9.81 × 0.6 = 17.66 N m.
α = 17.66/1.44 = 12.3 rad/s², which is 3g/(2L).
G then accelerates downwards at a_G = α(L/2) = 12.26 × 0.6 = 7.36 m/s².
Vertical forces: mg − R = m a_G, so R = 3(9.81 − 7.36) = 7.36 N upwards, which is a quarter of the weight. There is no horizontal reaction at this instant, because a_G has no horizontal component.

(b) The pin does no work, so mechanical energy is conserved. Between the horizontal and the vertical, G drops by L/2 = 0.6 m:
mg(L/2) = ½ I_O ω²
3 × 9.81 × 0.6 = 0.72ω²
ω² = 24.5, so ω = 4.95 rad/s, which matches √(3g/L).

(c) When the rod hangs vertically, the weight passes through O, so α = 0 and G has no tangential acceleration. Its acceleration is purely centripetal: ω²(L/2) = 24.5 × 0.6 = 14.7 m/s², directed up towards O.
R − mg = m ω²(L/2), so R = 3(9.81 + 14.7) = 73.6 N, which is 2.5mg.

Comment. During the swing, the pin reaction rises from a quarter of the weight at release to two and a half times the weight at the bottom. A pin or bearing sized only for the static weight of 29.4 N would be badly under-designed. This example shows why energy methods, which give ω, have to be combined with Newton's second law, which gives the forces, to find reactions that do no work.

questions.q: On a factory conveyor test rig, block P (2 kg) moving at 6 m/s collides head-on with block Q (3 kg), which is at rest on a smooth section. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5. After the impact Q moves onto a rough section where μk = 0.2. (a) Find the velocities of both blocks just after impact. (b) Find the kinetic energy lost in the impact. (c) Find how far Q slides on the rough section before stopping. (d) Explain why energy conservation could not be used for part (a). Take g = 9.81 m/s².
markScheme: Momentum: 2(6) = 2v_P + 3v_Q
Restitution: v_Q − v_P = 0.5 × 6 = 3
v_P = 0.6 m/s and v_Q = 3.6 m/s, both forward
Initial KE = 36 J
Energy is dissipated during impact unless e = 1; restitution supplies the second equation
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Take P's initial direction as positive. During the brief impact the only significant horizontal forces are the internal contact forces between the blocks, so linear momentum is conserved:
2 × 6 + 3 × 0 = 2v_P + 3v_Q, giving 12 = 2v_P + 3v_Q. (1)
Newton's experimental law says the separation speed is e times the approach speed:
v_Q − v_P = 0.5 × (6 − 0) = 3. (2)
Substitute v_Q = v_P + 3 into (1): 12 = 5v_P + 9, so v_P = 0.6 m/s and v_Q = 3.6 m/s. Both blocks move forward, and P follows more slowly.

(b) Kinetic energy before = ½ × 2 × 6² = 36.0 J.
Kinetic energy after = ½ × 2 × 0.6² + ½ × 3 × 3.6² = 0.36 + 19.44 = 19.8 J.
The loss is 16.2 J, which is 45% of the original kinetic energy. It goes into permanent deformation, heat and sound.

(c) On the rough section, kinetic friction F = 0.2 × 3 × 9.81 = 5.886 N removes Q's kinetic energy:
5.886 × d = 19.44, so d = 3.30 m.
Equivalently, the deceleration is μg = 1.962 m/s², and d = v²/(2μg) = 12.96/3.924 = 3.30 m.

(d) Mechanical energy is conserved in an impact only if e = 1. Here e = 0.5, so the collision dissipates energy that is not known in advance, and an energy balance would contain an unknown loss term. Momentum conservation holds whatever the losses, because the contact forces are equal and opposite. That gives one equation. The coefficient of restitution, an experimental property of the colliding surfaces, gives the second. Energy methods are appropriate again after the impact, as in part (c).

questions.q: A uniform rod of mass 4 kg and length 1.5 m hangs vertically from a frictionless pivot at its top end O. A 20 g projectile travelling horizontally at 300 m/s strikes the rod 1.2 m below O and embeds itself. (a) Find the angular velocity of the rod immediately after impact. (b) Find the percentage of kinetic energy lost. (c) Find the maximum angle through which the rod swings. (d) Find the horizontal impulse delivered by the pivot during impact, and show where the projectile would have to strike to make this impulse zero. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
markScheme: Conserve angular momentum about O, because the pivot impulse has no moment about O
H before = m v d = 0.02 × 300 × 1.2 = 7.2 kg m²/s
I after = ML²/3 + m d² = 3.0 + 0.0288 = 3.029 kg m²
KE before = 900 J; KE after = ½ I ω² = 8.56 J; 99.0% lost
Energy after impact: 8.56 = (MgL/2 + mg d)(1 − cos θ) = 29.67(1 − cos θ)
Momentum after = (M L/2 + m d)ω = 7.19 N s against 6.0 N s before
Pivot impulse = 1.19 N s, in the direction of the projectile's travel
Centre of percussion: zero pivot impulse when d = I_O/(M × L/2) = 2L/3 = 1.0 m (ignoring the projectile's own mass)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) During the very short impact, the pivot can apply a large impulsive force, so linear momentum is not conserved. That force acts through O, however, so angular momentum about O is conserved.
Before impact: H_O = m v d = 0.02 × 300 × 1.2 = 7.2 kg m²/s.
After impact the rod and embedded projectile rotate together, with I_O = ML²/3 + m d² = 4 × 2.25/3 + 0.02 × 1.44 = 3.0 + 0.0288 = 3.029 kg m².
ω = 7.2/3.029 = 2.38 rad/s.

(b) Kinetic energy before = ½ × 0.02 × 300² = 900 J. Kinetic energy after = ½ × 3.029 × 2.377² = 8.56 J. About 891 J, or 99.0%, is lost in the embedding process as heat and deformation.

(c) After impact the pivot does no work, so mechanical energy is conserved during the swing. As the rod swings through angle θ, G rises by (L/2)(1 − cos θ) and the projectile rises by d(1 − cos θ):
8.56 = (4 × 9.81 × 0.75 + 0.02 × 9.81 × 1.2)(1 − cos θ) = 29.67(1 − cos θ)
1 − cos θ = 0.2885, so θ = 44.6°.

(d) The linear momentum of the system just after impact is (M × L/2 + m d)ω = (3.0 + 0.024) × 2.377 = 7.19 N s. Just before impact it was 6.0 N s. The pivot must therefore have supplied a horizontal impulse of about 1.19 N s in the direction the projectile was travelling. The strike point (1.2 m below O) is below the centre of percussion (1.0 m below O), so without the pivot the top of the rod would kick backwards. The pivot therefore pushes the top of the rod forward.
Neglecting the projectile's small mass, the pivot impulse vanishes when the impulse J at depth d alone gives the correct momentum: J = M(L/2)ω and J d = I_O ω. Together these give d = I_O/(M L/2) = (ML²/3)/(ML/2) = 2L/3 = 1.0 m below O. This point is the centre of percussion, the same idea as the sweet spot of a bat.

questions.q: An instrument package of mass 5 kg is mounted on a spring of stiffness 2000 N/m with a viscous damper of coefficient 40 N s/m. It is displaced 10 mm from equilibrium and released from rest. (a) Find the undamped natural frequency, the critical damping coefficient and the damping ratio. (b) Find the damped natural frequency and the damped period. (c) Find the logarithmic decrement, and hence the ratio of successive peak amplitudes. (d) How many complete cycles pass before the amplitude falls below 1 mm? (e) What damper coefficient would give the quickest return to equilibrium without overshoot?
markScheme: ζ = 40/200 = 0.2, so underdamped
τd = 2π/ωd = 0.321 s
Successive peaks: x_n/x_(n+1) = e^δ = 3.61
n cycles reduce the amplitude by e^(nδ); need e^(nδ) ≥ 10, so n ≥ ln 10/δ = 1.80
After 2 complete cycles the peak is 10/3.61² = 0.77 mm < 1 mm
Critical damping c = 200 N s/m
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The undamped natural frequency is ωn = √(k/m) = √(2000/5) = 20 rad/s, or 3.18 Hz. The critical damping coefficient is c_c = 2√(km) = 2√(2000 × 5) = 200 N s/m. The damping ratio is ζ = c/c_c = 40/200 = 0.2. Since ζ < 1, the system is underdamped and will oscillate as it decays.

(b) The damped natural frequency is ωd = ωn√(1 − ζ²) = 20√0.96 = 19.6 rad/s. The damped period is τd = 2π/19.6 = 0.321 s. Damping of 20% reduces the frequency by only 2%.

(c) The logarithmic decrement is δ = 2πζ/√(1 − ζ²) = 2π(0.2)/0.980 = 1.283. The ratio of one peak to the next one in the same direction is e^1.283 = 3.61, so each cycle keeps only about 28% of the previous amplitude. The light-damping approximation 2πζ = 1.257 would be about 2% low here.

(d) After n complete cycles, the peak amplitude is 10 e^(−nδ) mm. For this to fall below 1 mm, e^(nδ) must exceed 10, so n > ln 10/1.283 = 1.80. The first positive peak after release is about 10/3.61 = 2.77 mm, and the second is 2.77/3.61 = 0.77 mm. The amplitude falls below 1 mm after two complete cycles, which takes about 0.64 s.

(e) The quickest return without overshoot comes from critical damping, ζ = 1, which needs c = c_c = 200 N s/m. That is five times the present value. In practice, instruments are often designed with ζ ≈ 0.6–0.7. This gives a small overshoot but a fast settling time and a flat frequency response.

questions.q: A 50 kg pump is bolted to rubber mounts with a total stiffness of 200 kN/m and a damping ratio of 0.1. An unbalanced impeller produces a harmonic vertical force of amplitude 500 N at 60 rad/s. Engineer Dana Okafor reports that the floor is vibrating badly. (a) Find the natural frequency and the frequency ratio. (b) Find the steady-state amplitude of the pump. (c) Find the transmissibility and the force amplitude transmitted to the floor. (d) Redesign the mounts so that the frequency ratio becomes √6. Find the new stiffness, the static deflection and the new transmitted force, keeping ζ = 0.1. (e) Discuss one drawback of the redesign and how to manage it.
markScheme: r = 60/63.2 = 0.949, close to resonance
F_T = 4.75 × 500 ≈ 2.37 kN, almost five times the applied force
New ωn = 60/√6 = 24.5 rad/s, so k = mωn² = 30 kN/m
Static deflection = mg/k = 16.4 mm
Drawback: passing through resonance at start-up and stop, plus larger static sag and rocking; manage with adequate damping, a quick run-up, motion limiters or an inertia block
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The natural frequency is ωn = √(k/m) = √(200,000/50) = 63.2 rad/s. The frequency ratio is r = 60/63.2 = 0.949. The pump runs very close to resonance, which explains the complaint.

(b) The static deflection under F₀ would be F₀/k = 500/200,000 = 2.5 mm. With 1 − r² = 0.100 and 2ζr = 0.190, the dynamic factor is 1/√(0.100² + 0.190²) = 1/0.2145 = 4.66. The steady-state amplitude is X = 2.5 × 4.66 = 11.7 mm.

(c) TR = √(1 + 0.190²)/0.2145 = 1.018/0.2145 = 4.75. The transmitted force amplitude is about 4.75 × 500 = 2.37 kN. The mounts are amplifying the force they were meant to isolate.

(d) For r = √6, the new natural frequency is ωn = 60/√6 = 24.5 rad/s. The stiffness must be k = mωn² = 50 × 600 = 30 kN/m. The static deflection becomes mg/k = 490.5/30,000 = 16.4 mm.
Now 1 − r² = −5 and 2ζr = 0.2 × 2.449 = 0.490. So TR = √(1 + 0.240)/√(25 + 0.240) = 1.113/5.024 = 0.222. The transmitted force falls to about 0.222 × 500 = 111 N, roughly a twentieth of the present value. Ignoring damping would give TR = 1/(r² − 1) = 0.20, which shows that damping slightly worsens isolation in this region. The pump amplitude would be (500/30,000)/5.024 = 3.3 mm.

(e) The softer mounts put ωn below the running speed, so the pump must pass through resonance every time it starts and stops. During these transients, large amplitudes and forces can build up, especially if the run-up is slow. The extra 16 mm of static sag can also overstress pipe connections and allow rocking. To manage this, keep enough damping (ζ around 0.1 to 0.2), use a drive that accelerates quickly through 24.5 rad/s, fit snubbers or motion limiters, and add flexible pipe couplings. Mounting the pump on a heavy inertia block also lowers the centre of gravity and reduces the amplitude.

questions.q: "For any problem in particle or rigid-body dynamics, energy methods are superior to the direct application of Newton's second law." Critically assess this statement. Refer to specific types of problem, and to the limitations of each approach.
markScheme: States the work–energy principle and Newton's second law correctly
Energy is a scalar, so there is no vector resolution and it works well for connected systems and speed–position questions
Workless constraint forces drop out, which is efficient
Energy cannot give forces that do no work (pin reactions, normal forces)
Energy gives speed, not direction, and gives time only indirectly
Energy fails across impacts, where impulse–momentum and restitution are needed
Non-conservative forces need their work known in advance; path-dependent friction complicates things
Newton's second law gives instantaneous accelerations and forces, and is needed for slip or tip checks
Hybrid use: energy for ω, then ΣF = m a_G for reactions, as in the rod example
Reasoned conclusion: methods are complementary, chosen by what is unknown
questions.modelAnswer:
The statement overstates the case. The work–energy principle, T₁ + V₁ + U_nc = T₂ + V₂, and Newton's second law, ΣF = m a_G with ΣM_G = I_G α, are the same physics. The first is the second integrated over displacement. Each is more efficient for particular unknowns.

Energy methods have clear strengths. Energy is a scalar, so no resolution of components is needed. Workless forces, such as smooth normal reactions, fixed pins, internal string tensions and static friction in rolling, never appear. For a connected system, a single equation relates speed to position without solving for intermediate tensions. Finding the speed of a block that has compressed a spring, or the angular velocity of a falling rod, takes one line.

The same feature is also a weakness. Because workless forces vanish, energy cannot find them. To find the pin reaction on a swinging rod, or the normal force on a car at the top of a loop, you need ΣF = m a_G with the centripetal term. Energy gives speed but not direction, and it gives time only through a further integration. It cannot be applied across an impact or plastic deformation, where the loss is unknown. There, impulse–momentum with a coefficient of restitution, or angular momentum about a pivot, takes over. Non-conservative work must be known in advance, which is awkward when friction depends on a normal force that is itself changing.

Newton's second law gives instantaneous accelerations and forces. That makes it essential for checking whether a body slips or tips, for problems where friction changes from static to kinetic, and for setting up differential equations of motion, as in vibrations. It is more laborious for long paths and systems with many bodies.

Good practice combines the two. Use energy to find v or ω at a position, then use Newton's second law to find forces, and use momentum methods for impacts. The best method depends on what is unknown (a speed, a force or a time), not on any general superiority of one approach.
